topic.title: Ghost Demand: Are State-Level Interconnection Queue Freezes the AI Buildout's New Power Bottleneck?
topic.trigger: Texas Governor Greg Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT on August 3, 2026 to freeze all new data-center grid interconnections pending a comprehensive statewide audit, after requests reached approximately 474 gigawatts -- over five times Texas's record peak demand -- with regulators and a Reuters review attributing most of the gap to duplicative, speculative 'ghost demand' filings; Pennsylvania (Executive Order 2026-05, August 18) and Ohio (AEP Ohio tariff) have imposed comparable queue-integrity controls, and a Reuters review found over 700 gigawatts of similar large-load requests nationally -- a genuinely new administrative/regulatory bottleneck mechanism distinct from this pipeline's prior August 2026 reports on political-opposition moratoria and PJM's BYONC curtailment-priority framework.

questions.primary: Texas's Governor Abbott froze all new data-center grid interconnections in August 2026 pending an audit of roughly 474 gigawatts of requests -- over five times the state's peak demand -- and Pennsylvania, Ohio and other states have imposed comparable speculative-demand controls. Is this administrative 'ghost demand' gatekeeping now a binding near-term constraint on new AI data-center power capacity, distinct from the physical equipment shortages and political-opposition moratoria this pipeline has already tracked, and if so, how long is it likely to bind before queues are cleaned up or projects reroute to less-restrictive states?
sub: How large is the gap between headline interconnection-queue gigawatts and verified, financed demand nationally and in Texas specifically, and what does that reveal about the reliability of the 474GW/700GW figures?
What are ERCOT's and Pennsylvania's actual audit and verification timelines, and when might new interconnections resume at pre-freeze pace?

Are major hyperscalers (Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, OpenAI) responding to the freeze by rerouting capital to unaffected states, or by pursuing behind-the-meter/dedicated-generation deals such as Vistra's Comanche Peak arrangement with Amazon?

Is this queue-integrity freeze a genuinely new bottleneck mechanism, or an acceleration of the political-opposition and curtailment-priority dynamics this pipeline already identified in its August 2026 moratorium and PJM BYONC reports?

Does the strict Structural Bottleneck test (demand High/Extreme + supply elasticity Low + substitutability Hard) hold for state-level interconnection-queue gatekeeping capacity, or is this better classified as a temporary Growth-Area friction given behind-the-meter workarounds and self-correcting queue cleanup?

thesis: Since August 2026, Texas (via Governor Abbott's August 3 directive to ERCOT/PUCT), Pennsylvania (Executive Order 2026-05, August 18) and Ohio (AEP Ohio's data-center tariff) have moved to freeze or gate new data-center grid interconnections in response to 'ghost demand': a Reuters review found electricity requests from large power users, overwhelmingly data centers, exceeding 700 gigawatts nationally and 474 gigawatts in Texas alone (over five times Texas's record peak demand and roughly a tenfold increase since 2023), with regulators and consumer advocates attributing much of this to duplicative or unfunded speculative filings rather than real, financed demand. This is a distinct bottleneck mechanism from the political-opposition moratoria and PJM curtailment-priority rules this pipeline covered in August 2026: it is an administrative queue-integrity and verification problem, not a physical equipment shortage or a community-opposition veto. The freeze is real and immediate -- ERCOT has paused its Batch Zero classification process and up to roughly 1,800 Texas projects are reported halted pending audit -- but the evidence suggests it functions more as a temporary, self-correcting friction than a hard structural constraint: ERCOT targets audit completion around December 2026, Pennsylvania's order explicitly favors projects that bring their own generation, and Vistra's dedicated Comanche Peak nuclear supply to Amazon shows large players can route around the general public queue via bespoke arrangements. Supply elasticity in queue-processing capacity is low in the near term, but substitutability via behind-the-meter and dedicated-supply deals is real, which weighs against classifying this as a proven Structural Bottleneck even as it materially slows the pace of new interconnection approvals in the near term.

facts.statement: On August 3, 2026, Texas Governor Greg Abbott sent a letter directing the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and ERCOT to conduct a 'comprehensive verification and audit' of all data centers advancing through ERCOT's interconnection process, stating that any project found in violation of applicable requirements 'must be denied connection to the Texas grid,' and that no additional data center may be approved to move forward in the interconnection process until the audit is complete.

Abbott's letter stated ERCOT was considering approximately 474 gigawatts of interconnection requests, roughly 90% of which are data centers -- more than five times Texas's record peak electricity demand, up from about 48 gigawatts of such requests in 2023.

ERCOT immediately paused its 'Batch Zero' large-load interconnection classification and study process in response, seeking a good-cause exception from the PUC on the process's original August 7, 2026 deadline; ERCOT has stated it aims to complete the governor-directed audit by around December 2026.

A Reuters review of utility and grid data found electricity requests from very large power users, overwhelmingly data centers, exceeding 700 gigawatts across the Midwest, Mid-Atlantic and South -- more than ten times current industry estimates of actual U.S. data-center power consumption; outside Texas, ten major utilities including AEP Ohio, Southern Co. and PPL have logged roughly 270 gigawatts of large-load requests.

Consumer advocates and regulators attribute much of the gap to 'ghost demand': developers filing speculative, often duplicative interconnection requests at multiple utilities for the same eventual campus at low cost, without identified financing or firm customers; some utilities have seen reported demand fall sharply once financial guardrails such as upfront payments were imposed.

AEP Ohio's data-center tariff, which requires prospective customers to pay a load-study fee of roughly $10,000-$100,000 and meet contractual commitments, is reported to have cut AEP Ohio's data-center interconnection pipeline by more than half as speculative or duplicative projects dropped out.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed Executive Order 2026-05 on August 18, 2026, applying stricter permitting and disclosure ('GRID') requirements to data centers with peak demand above 25 megawatts, including phased clean-firm-energy requirements starting at 10% in 2027 and rising to 32% by 2035, and giving preferential treatment to projects that bring their own generation or storage over speculative campuses without secured power or customers.

Of more than 100 data centers proposed in Pennsylvania, only about 20 had applied for the permits needed to move projects forward as of the order, and most proposals had not secured power sources or a committed customer.

At least 43 companies, including Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft and Amazon Web Services, issued public statements supporting Abbott's audit directive; the Data Center Coalition urged PUCT and ERCOT to 'move swiftly' to distinguish speculative projects from serious, committed investors.

As of mid-August 2026, up to roughly 1,800 Texas data-center-related interconnection projects were reported halted pending the audit, with more projects reported complying with Abbott's directive over time.

Independent power producer Vistra Corp. publicly supported the Texas pause and said it does not expect the audit to affect its existing 1.2-gigawatt agreement to supply an Amazon data center directly from its Comanche Peak nuclear plant.

ERCOT's system-wide steady-state and stability screening study is expected to produce Year 1-6 MW interconnection allocations by April 9, 2027, with a refinement study identifying recommended transmission improvements by June 1, 2027, and a final transmission plan expected in fall 2027.

Growth in existing and forecast data-center demand is estimated to have driven a $29.4 billion increase in capacity costs for homes and businesses within the PJM footprint over roughly the past four capacity auctions.
Texas data-center electricity demand is projected to grow from about 7.4 gigawatts in 2026 to 228.4 gigawatts by 2032 under one industry estimate cited alongside coverage of the ERCOT queue freeze.

inferences.statement: Because the headline 474GW (Texas) and 700GW (national) interconnection-request figures are reported by regulators and Reuters to be dominated by duplicative or unfunded speculative filings rather than financed demand, the effective near-term supply constraint is less about physical grid capacity than about the states' and utilities' administrative capacity to verify which requests are real -- a distinct mechanism from the equipment-shortage and political-opposition bottlenecks this pipeline covered in August 2026.

Because Vistra's dedicated Comanche Peak-Amazon supply arrangement and Pennsylvania's explicit preference for bring-your-own-generation projects both predate and survive the freezes, large, well-capitalized developers appear able to substitute bespoke, direct-supply deals for the general public interconnection queue -- evidence against 'Hard' substitutability and against classifying queue-gatekeeping capacity as a proven Structural Bottleneck.

Because ERCOT has set a rough December 2026 target for completing its audit and a concrete April-to-fall 2027 timeline for resuming systematic interconnection allocation, the Texas freeze looks more like a multi-quarter administrative pause than an open-ended structural constraint, though the timeline could slip given the audit's acknowledged lack of procedural specifics as of mid-August 2026.

Because AEP Ohio's tariff-driven verification process is reported to have already cut its data-center pipeline by more than half, queue-integrity problems appear substantially self-correcting once utilities impose financial guardrails (study fees, upfront payments) -- suggesting the 'ghost demand' bottleneck resolves faster than physical capacity bottlenecks such as transformers or turbines, which require years of lead time.

Because at least 43 major hyperscalers publicly endorsed rather than opposed Abbott's audit, the largest, best-financed developers appear to see the freeze as a way to clear out lower-quality speculative competitors for scarce interconnection capacity -- implying the policy response may ultimately concentrate, rather than reduce, available interconnection capacity among incumbent large players.

unknowns: No source disclosed what share of the 474GW Texas queue or the 700GW national figure is ultimately expected to survive verification as real, financed demand; estimates of the 'ghost' share were qualitative, not quantified.

No source confirmed whether ERCOT's Batch Zero process, once resumed, will process the backlog on a first-in-line or a re-ranked basis, which would materially affect which specific projects are delayed longest.

Whether other major data-center states (Virginia, Georgia, Arizona) will adopt comparable queue-verification freezes, or whether developers are already reallocating capital toward such unaffected states, was not confirmed by available sources.
The precise magnitude of any capital reallocation away from Texas and Pennsylvania toward states without comparable audits was not found in available sources.

Every primary-source domain attempted for direct verification in this research session (gov.texas.gov, pa.gov, utilitydive.com, texastribune.org, ercot.com) was blocked by the research environment's egress proxy; facts rely on convergent search-result snippets rather than direct page fetches.

bottlenecks.node: State/ISO interconnection-queue verification & audit capacity (Texas, Pennsylvania, Ohio)
bottlenecks.expansion_time: months, roughly Q3 2026 through the ERCOT audit's December 2026 target and April-fall 2027 systematic allocation timeline
bottlenecks.rationale: Demand for interconnection (474GW Texas, 700GW national) is extreme and regulators' verification/audit throughput is genuinely limited in the near term (Low elasticity). But substitutability is only Medium, not Hard: large developers can and do route around the general queue via bespoke behind-the-meter or dedicated-generation deals (Vistra-Amazon), and Pennsylvania's rules explicitly reward that path. Combined with a concrete multi-quarter timeline to audit completion and resumed processing, this falls short of the strict Structural Bottleneck test and is better classified a Growth Area friction that materially slows, but does not durably block, new AI data-center power access.

bear_case.argument: The freeze is an administrative, state-level action with concrete target dates (audit by ~December 2026, allocations by April 2027); it is inherently more reversible and shorter-duration than physical equipment shortages such as transformers or gas turbines that require years of lead time.

As of mid-August 2026, the Texas Tribune reported the audit 'lacks specifics' -- no confirmed scope, duration, or methodology -- raising the risk it functions more as political messaging than a rigorous or durable gatekeeping mechanism.

Regulators and Reuters attribute much of the 474GW/700GW figures to duplicative or unfunded speculative filings rather than real demand; if verified demand turns out to be a small fraction of the headline number, the 'bottleneck' framing overstates genuine supply-demand tightness.

43 major hyperscalers publicly supported the audit rather than opposing it, and AEP Ohio's comparable tariff already cut its pipeline by more than half without apparent harm to committed projects -- suggesting incumbent, well-financed developers may benefit from (not be constrained by) queue cleanup at the expense of smaller speculative entrants.

Vistra's dedicated Comanche Peak-Amazon deal and Pennsylvania's bring-your-own-generation preference show that well-capitalized developers can substitute private, bespoke supply arrangements for the general interconnection queue, undercutting the 'Hard substitutability' condition needed for a genuine structural bottleneck.

kill_conditions.condition: ERCOT completes its audit substantially on schedule (around December 2026) and clears a large majority of queued projects, resuming Batch Zero processing at or near its pre-freeze pace
kill_conditions.metric: Share of audited Texas interconnection requests cleared and Batch Zero resumption date
kill_conditions.threshold: Audit completed within 1-2 months of the ~December 2026 target with resumed processing

kill_conditions.condition: Verified, financed demand within the audited queue turns out to be a large majority (e.g., >50%) of the original 474GW headline figure, showing the 'ghost demand' framing overstated the actual gap
kill_conditions.metric: Disclosed verified vs. total requested capacity
kill_conditions.threshold: Verified demand exceeds roughly half of headline requested capacity

kill_conditions.condition: Multiple additional major data-center states (e.g., Virginia, Georgia, Arizona) adopt comparable interconnection-queue freezes or audits, confirming a durable national pattern rather than a Texas/Pennsylvania/Ohio-specific response
kill_conditions.metric: Number of states adopting comparable queue-verification measures
kill_conditions.threshold: 2 or more additional major data-center states within 2-3 quarters

kill_conditions.condition: Disclosed evidence that hyperscalers are reallocating a material share of planned Texas/Pennsylvania capital expenditure to unaffected states or to behind-the-meter deals because of the freeze
kill_conditions.metric: Disclosed capital reallocation away from frozen-queue states
kill_conditions.threshold: Any material, named reallocation disclosed by a major hyperscaler or developer
